reason: REFUTED on translation drift, which is exactly what the verifier admitted it had not checked: it never opened the 1964 Simms volume and leaned on Wikiquote. The wording proposed is not Ruth L. C. Simms’s. It is James E. Irby’s. Two independent checks. First, I downloaded a scan of Labyrinths: Selected Stories and Other Writings (ed. Yates and Irby, New Directions) and read the essay: the closing paragraph runs “...it is frightful because it is irreversible and iron-clad. Time is the substance I am made of. Time is a river which sweeps me along, but I am the river; it is a tiger which destroys me, but I am the tiger; it is a fire which consumes me, but I am the fire. The world, unfortunately, is real; I, unfortunately, am Borges.” The essay carries the credit “Translated by J.E.I.” at its foot. That is the proposed sentence, letter for letter, semicolons and all. Second, the Simms text reads differently at both hinges: Bruno Bosteels, The Jargon of Finitude (Radical Philosophy), quotes it and cites Other Inquisitions 1937–1952, trans. Ruth L. C. Simms, University of Texas Press, 1964, p. 187, as “Time is the substance I am made of. Time is a river that carries me away, but I am the river; it is a tiger that mangles me, but I am the tiger; it is a fire that consumes me, but I am the fire.” Simms has “that carries me away” and “that mangles me” where the proposal has “which sweeps me along” and “which destroys me”. Only the first sentence is common to both, which is why a reference lookup that matches on “Time is the substance I am made of” lands on the wrong book. So the card as proposed would print Irby’s English under Simms’s name and year: a confident false citation of precisely the kind the standard forbids. Everything else about the line is clean. Borges is not banned and stands at 0 of 3; shipped.js finds neither the line nor a near opening; the Spanish original is 1944 to 1946 and both translations are early 1960s, so it is in scope; Essay is the form; it is publishable and it sits squarely on impermanence. The fix is only to name the translation the wording actually belongs to, which is what betterCitation does at 107 characters, no dash, no straight quote. If the editor would rather keep Simms, the quotation must be re-set in Simms’s words and the locator given as Other Inquisitions, p. 187, but that should not be done from my report alone: it wants the printed page.
betterCitation: Jorge Luis Borges, Labyrinths, A New Refutation of Time, the closing paragraph (trans. James E. Irby, 1962)
